bigPicture: Number sets form a hierarchy **ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ**; irrational numbers fill the gaps in ℚ.
**Σ-notation** compresses long sums; linearity rules and **Gauss' formula** simplify them.
Solving inequalities: track the direction and **flip the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative number** (“the #1 mistake”).
**Absolute value** = distance from 0; solve with cases or the standard equivalences.

concepts.name: Number sets
concepts.simple: Counting numbers (ℕ), plus negatives (ℤ), plus fractions (ℚ), plus everything on the number line (ℝ).
exam: - **ℝ**: all points on the number line, rational and irrational
- **ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ**. Domains, solution sets and intervals are described as subsets of these.

concepts.name: Summation notation (Σ)
concepts.simple: Σ is a short way to write ‘add up all these terms’: the index i runs from the bottom number to the top number.
exam: **Definition:** Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ aᵢ = a₁ + a₂ + ⋯ + aₙ; i is the **index**, running from the lower limit 1 to the upper limit n.
**Rules:** Σ(aᵢ + bᵢ) = Σaᵢ + Σbᵢ · Σ c·aᵢ = c·Σaᵢ · Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ c = n·c

concepts.name: Rational, irrational and real numbers
concepts.simple: Rational numbers are fractions; their decimals stop or repeat. Irrational numbers (√2, π, e) have endless decimals that never repeat.
exam: - **Rational:** p/q with p, q ∈ ℤ, q ≠ 0; decimal expansion **finite or eventually periodic** (0.75 = 3/4, 0.3̄ = 1/3). **Integers are rational** (p = p/1).
- **Irrational:** not rational; decimal expansion **infinite and non-periodic**: √2, π, e.
- **ℝ = ℚ ∪ {irrational numbers}**: the real line has no gaps.
- **Proof idea that √2 is irrational:** if √2 = p/q in lowest terms, then p² = 2q² forces both p and q to be even – contradicting lowest terms.
concepts.example: “Every integer is rational” is true (q = 1); “every rational is an integer” is false (1/2).

concepts.name: Rules for inequalities
concepts.simple: You can add the same number to both sides, and multiply by a positive number. If you multiply or divide by a negative number, the arrow turns around.
exam: - a < b ⇔ a + c < b + c (adding preserves the direction)
- a < b and b < c ⇒ a < c (**transitivity**)

concepts.name: Rational inequalities with a sign table
concepts.simple: Find where the top and the bottom are zero, then check the sign of each part on every interval. The bottom can never be zero.
exam: Solve (x − 1)/(x + 2) ≥ 0: zero of numerator x = 1; zero of denominator (**excluded**) x = −2.

concepts.name: Absolute value: equations and inequalities
concepts.simple: |x| is the distance of x from 0, so it is never negative. |x| = 5 means x is 5 or −5.
exam: **Definition:** |x| = x if x ≥ 0, and |x| = −x if x < 0. Geometrically the distance from 0; |a − b| is the distance between a and b.

connections: **Session 1:** number sets are sets; solution sets use ∪ and intervals.
**Session 3:** natural domains require inequalities (denominator ≠ 0, root argument ≥ 0).
**Math A Lecture 1:** Σ-notation for series; Gauss' formula proved by induction.

questions: Evaluate sums in Σ-notation; use Gauss' formula.
Solve linear inequalities (watch the flip) and rational inequalities (sign table).
True/false questions on ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, ℝ and irrational numbers.
traps: Multiplying/dividing by a negative number **flips** the inequality.
Never multiply a rational inequality by the denominator without knowing its sign – use a sign table.
Zeros of the denominator are **always excluded**; zeros of the numerator included only for ≥ / ≤.
Σ from i = 0 has one more term than from i = 1.
mistakes: Writing |x| > c as −c > x > c (impossible) instead of x < −c **or** x > c.
Claiming 0.3̄ is irrational (it is periodic, so rational).

memorize: **Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ i = n(n + 1)/2;** Σ c = n·c; Σ c·aᵢ = c·Σ aᵢ.

practice.question: Which number is irrational?
practice.explanation: √2 has an infinite, non-periodic decimal expansion.

practice.question: Which statement is FALSE?
options: Every rational number is an integer.
practice.explanation: 1/2 is rational but not an integer.

options: p² = 2q² forces p and q both even, contradicting lowest terms
Because 2 is prime and √ of a prime is an integer

questions.explanation: Multiplying by a negative number flips the sign.

questions.question: Solution of (2x + 1)/(x − 3) < 0:
questions.explanation: Numerator positive and denominator negative between −1/2 and 3.

questions.question: Solve (x − 1)/(x + 2) ≥ 0 with a sign table. State the solution as an interval and say which boundary points are included.
questions.model:
Zero of the numerator x = 1; zero of the denominator x = −2 (excluded).
x < −2: (−)/(−) = + · −2 < x < 1: (−)/(+) = − · x > 1: (+)/(+) = +.
Solution: x ∈ (−∞, −2) ∪ [1, ∞); −2 excluded (division by 0), 1 included (quotient = 0 satisfies ≥).

keyPoints.text: Correct signs on all three intervals

questions.question: Define rational and irrational numbers via their decimal expansion and give two examples of each.
questions.model: Rational: p/q with p, q ∈ ℤ, q ≠ 0; decimal expansion finite or eventually periodic (e.g. 0.75 = 3/4, 0.3̄ = 1/3, any integer). Irrational: not rational; infinite, non-periodic expansion (e.g. √2, π, e).
